display.purpose: Page-level h1 and h2 only. Piazzolla with optical sizing left automatic, at weight 580 — lighter than Title because it is set twice the size. Size is set by the surface, not by a token.

title.purpose: Card titles — the only place the display face appears inside a component. Weight 640, heavier than Display so that at 1.25rem it reads as the same weight.

body.purpose: Running text and input values, Sofia Sans at an untuned 400. The 1.55 leading is what keeps dense forms breathable.

label.purpose: Field labels, button text, and descriptions. Weight 580 — just under semibold, so a label is findable without being loud.

micro.purpose: Badges and small keys. Weight 760 and tight-leaded: at 0.75rem in all-caps there are no ascenders or descenders left, so weight is the only surviving hierarchy signal.

code.purpose: Inline code and code blocks, in Lilex. Inline is 0.8em relative to its parent; blocks are 0.875rem absolute. Lilex is bundled rather than left to a system monospace stack, which was three different faces with three different x-heights depending on the reader's platform.

shadows.name: plate
shadows.purpose: A card or panel resting on the plate. Light mode only — resolves to none in dark and under forced-colors. Tinted with graphite ink rather than black.

shadows.name: overlay
shadows.purpose: Popovers and select menus in light mode. The only shadow that survives into dark, where it deepens to 0 18px 44px rgb(0 0 0 / 0.45).

shadows.name: overlay-dark
shadows.purpose: The dark-mode overlay cast. Detachment must stay legible in both physics.

shadows.name: selected-marker
shadows.purpose: The mint marker on a selected select option. A marker rather than a fill, so selection and focus can coexist without fighting.

motion.name: press
motion.purpose: The key press: transform, border-block-end-width, and background-color transition together as one gesture. Also the select chevron rotation.

motion.name: popover-in
motion.purpose: Popover and select menu entrance — opacity from 0 with a 4px rise. Removed entirely under prefers-reduced-motion.

motion.name: reduced-motion-floor
motion.purpose: Under prefers-reduced-motion, all transition and animation durations collapse to 0.01ms and the key press re-expresses itself as a fill change to coral-edge rather than travel.

components.name: Primary Button
components.description: The committing action. A coral keycap with a 4px side wall that compresses as the cap travels.

components.name: Card
components.description: The plate itself. Largest radius in the system, divider-weight border, and the only component that casts a plate shadow.

Release checklist

Every item is verified before a component reaches stable.

narrative.overview:
Keycaps is a plate, and a small number of solid objects seated on it. The plate is the protagonist: a warm near-white ground (cloud #f5f5f3) that asks for nothing, holds everything, and stays quiet under whatever is placed on it. Objects that sit on the plate are unmistakably objects — they have a border, a radius, a bottom edge, and a shadow that says they occupy space rather than float above it. Nothing dissolves into the page.

The system is tactile but restrained. It contains real physical feedback, and it spends it almost nowhere. A primary key travels 3px on press while its 4px bottom edge compresses to 1px, so the cap descends and bottoms out while its lower boundary stays exactly where it was — the motion of a key hitting the plate beneath it. That press is the single most expressive thing the system does, it lasts 120ms, and it is the reason the rest of the interface holds still. If everything moved, the press would mean nothing.

Warmth comes from material, not from saturation. The neutrals are warm-shifted rather than gray (plate #fdfdfb, divider #e7e7e3), the display face is Piazzolla drawing itself for the size it is set at over a quiet Sofia Sans, and the accent is coral rather than blue. Coral appears at full strength on exactly one kind of thing — an action that commits — which is why the plate reads as calm. The scarcity is semantic, not budgeted: commitments are rare, so the color that marks them is rare.
keyCharacteristics: Warm near-white ground; nothing is pure gray and nothing is pure white
Objects are seated, not floating — border, radius, and edge are the default vocabulary
One expressive gesture (the 120ms key press) surrounded by stillness
Coral marks commitment; every other status speaks in mint, mustard, or signal blue
Depth is cast in light and tonal in dark — the same object, two different physics
Every state has a non-color carrier, because forced-colors and screen readers are release gates

rules.name: The Commitment Rule
rules.body: The coral key face is worn only by actions that commit or confirm. Multiple commitments on one screen may all wear it — coral marks a kind of action, not a rank. The plate stays quiet because genuine commitments are rare, not because a budget caps them.

rules.name: The Tone Trio Rule
rules.body: Every status tone sets surface, border, and text together. A tone expressed by only one of the three is incomplete, and a status expressed by color alone is a defect — there is always a label, an icon, or a role carrying the same meaning.

rules.name: The Warm Neutral Rule
rules.body: No pure grays, no #000, no #fff. Every neutral in the system carries a warm or cool bias; a value with equal RGB channels has escaped the palette.

rules.name: The Two Voice Rule
rules.body: Piazzolla speaks in page headings and card titles. Sofia Sans does everything else — every label, every value, every button, every error. Lilex speaks only in code. Piazzolla creeping into body copy breaks the system, and three faces is the ceiling: display, body, code.

rules.name: The Optical Sizing Rule
rules.body: Piazzolla's opsz axis is never pinned. It runs on font-optical-sizing: auto, so the face draws itself for the size it is set at, and there is no font-variation-settings anywhere in the system. Its range of 8–30 spans a 1.25rem card title through a 2.5rem page heading; pinning it would trade away the small-size drawing that makes the Title role work. Replaces the Optical Constant Rule, which pinned the previous display face's SOFT and WONK axes.

rules.name: The Optical Weight Rule
rules.body: Roles carry the weight they need, not the nearest hundred. Apparent stroke weight falls as size falls, so a single number spanning a 40px heading and a 12px badge does not read as one system. Display sits at 580 and Title at 640 — the same intent at twice the size apart, bracketing 600 rather than sharing it. Label is 580, findable without being loud. Micro carries 760 because 12px uppercase has no ascenders or descenders left to help it. Body is deliberately untuned at 400. The generic ladder (400/500/600/700) remains for consumers; both faces are variable, so every rung is a real weight in both voices.

rules.name: The Inline Code Rule
rules.body: Code is set in Lilex at --kc-font-size-code (0.8em), relative to its parent rather than on the size ramp, because it appears inside body, label and table text alike. Code blocks take --kc-font-size-code-block (0.875rem) instead: a block has no surrounding prose to match. The size is doing work a face cannot — monospace convention is a ~0.6em advance against Sofia Sans' ~0.41em average, and every monospace candidate measured on this system landed at 0.6em. What a face can fix is apparent size: the previous system stack set a 0.547em x-height against the body's 0.488em, so code read a size larger than its surroundings. Lilex sets 0.516em. Bundling it also ends a quieter problem — a system stack is not one face, and the pairing had only ever been judged on macOS.

rules.name: Dark mode shaves weight.
rules.body: Light glyphs on a dark ground irradiate: the bright stroke bleeds into its surround and reads heavier than the same weight on white. Every role weight is calc(base + var(--kc-font-weight-shift)), where the shift is 0 in light and -20 in dark. Only a variable face can do this. The direction is a judgment about these two faces — both are low-contrast enough that irradiation, rather than thin strokes breaking up, dominates; a high-contrast face would want the opposite sign.

rules.name: The No Faux Type Rule
rules.body: font-synthesis: none is on, so the browser never fakes a weight or a slant. Shipped coverage is the real contract. Sofia Sans is variable across its whole range in both upright and italic, so every weight and every emphasis combination in the body voice is real — including emphasis inside bold copy, which under the previous static body face fell back to upright. Piazzolla ships upright only, so italic inside a heading still renders upright rather than being synthesized.

rules.name: The Heading Rhythm Rule
rules.body: A heading gets more space above it than below — --kc-space-heading-above (1.6em) against --kc-space-heading-below (0.6em), a ratio near 2.67:1, so the heading belongs to the section it opens rather than the one it closes. Both values are em, so they scale with whatever size the surface chose. Spatial contrast is doing real hierarchy work here: the size ramp steps by a constant 0.125rem, so its largest ratio is 1.167:1 — below the threshold at which a size change reads as a role change on its own.

rules.name: The 320 Rule
rules.body: Every surface reflows at 320 CSS pixels with no horizontal page scroll. html and body carry min-width: 320px as the floor, and it is verified in the browser matrix — not a guideline, a release gate.

rules.name: The Intrinsic Maximum Rule
rules.body: Components declare their own measure ceiling with min(100%, Xrem). Never constrain a Keycaps component from the outside when it already knows its comfortable width.

rules.name: The Light Lifts, Dark Layers Rule
rules.body: Cast shadow belongs to light mode. In dark mode, depth comes from surface tone alone. Adding a plate shadow to a dark surface is a defect, not an enhancement.

rules.name: The Overlay Exception Rule
rules.body: Only genuinely detached surfaces — popovers, select menus, dialogs — cast in both themes. If it rests on the plate, it does not cast in dark.

rules.name: The Pressable Edge Rule
rules.body: A bottom edge promises travel. Anything wearing a border-block-end heavier than its other borders must depress when activated. A static element with a weighted bottom edge is a false affordance.

rules.name: The Leading Edge Rule
rules.body: A heavier border-inline-start marks a block that is quoted from or attributed to something outside the flow — a Banner's tone, a callout, a blockquote, a samp showing real program output. It is the one place the system uses a weighted side border, always on the inline-start edge so it flips for RTL, and never decoration. Deliberately not the keycap's bottom edge: that promises travel and belongs to things that depress, while a leading edge promises provenance and belongs to things that do not move. A considered exception to the general advice against colored side borders, because the convention predates the system and the alternative is spending a second color to say the same thing.

rules.name: The Concentric Radius Rule
rules.body: A nested corner is the parent's radius minus the gap between them, computed with calc(). Never restate a nested radius as a literal.

dos: Do couple the press values. translateY(3px) and the 4px → 1px edge compression are one gesture; changing either alone breaks the key's physics.
Do give every status a second carrier. Surface, border, and text move together, and a label, icon, or ARIA role carries the meaning when color is unavailable.
Do compute nested radii with calc() from the parent (calc(var(--kc-radius-key) - 3px)), so curves stay concentric.
Do let components set their own measure with min(100%, Xrem) rather than constraining them from outside.
Do reach for semantic tokens (--kc-color-key-face, --kc-color-danger-text) in component CSS. Brand primitives are the palette's source, not its interface.
Do express every state change in a way that survives forced-colors: active — the system already maps every semantic token to a system color, and new components must too.
Do use logical properties (inline-size, border-block-end, padding-inline) so the system flips for RTL for free.
donts: Don't drift toward borderless flat minimalism — shadowless cards, seamless surfaces, objects that dissolve into the page. Keycaps is built on things being seated and visibly distinct from their ground. This is the system's confirmed anti-reference.
Don't put a weighted bottom edge on something that doesn't depress. The edge promises travel; a static element wearing one is a false affordance.
Don't add a plate shadow in dark mode. Depth there is the surface ladder, not a cast.
Don't use coral for anything but a committing action. Not for emphasis, not for decoration, not for a hover state on something that isn't a key.
Don't introduce a fourth typeface, or let Piazzolla into body copy. Three faces is the ceiling: display, body, code.
Don't pin Piazzolla's opsz axis, per surface or globally. Optical sizing runs automatically; fixing it to one value breaks the Title role.
Don't write raw color values in component CSS. If a needed color has no token, add the token.
Don't fetch anything at runtime — fonts, styles, or icons. Everything ships with the package.
Don't remove or restyle the focus ring below 3px at 3px offset.
Don't use pure gray, pure black, or pure white. Every neutral carries a bias.
Don't set symmetric margins on a heading, or leave it on the UA default, which is symmetric. More space above than below is what makes a heading read as opening its section.
Don't pin Piazzolla's opsz axis, and don't put a weighted side border on anything that is not quoting or attributing.
